title: Goodput
short_definition: A serving metric counting only completed requests per second that meet their latency SLOs (TTFT and ITL targets), unlike raw throughput which counts every request regardless of speed.
full_explanation: Raw throughput is a vanity number for interactive serving. If you push batch sizes up to maximize tokens per second, tail latency climbs, and past some point requests still complete but miss their deadlines — a user waiting four seconds for the first token got a response the product treats as a failure. Goodput fixes this by counting only the requests that satisfy the latency contract, typically a time-to-first-token bound plus an inter-token-latency bound. It reframes capacity planning around the experience you actually promised rather than the work the GPU happened to do. A request enters with an SLO, for example TTFT under 2 seconds and ITL under 50 milliseconds. The scheduler serves it inside whatever batch is currently running. After completion you check both deadlines; if either is violated the request counts toward throughput but not goodput. Sweeping the maximum batch size shows the tradeoff directly — larger batches raise raw throughput but eventually depress goodput as more requests blow their latency budget. The operating point that maximizes goodput is often a smaller batch than the one that maximizes throughput, which is the counterintuitive result the metric exists to surface.
why_it_matters: Throughput and user experience diverge under load, and optimizing the wrong one quietly ships a slow product. Goodput is the number that ties capacity, batching, and autoscaling decisions to the SLO you sell. Disaggregated-serving papers report their wins in goodput precisely because colocated prefill and decode inflate throughput while violating tail latency.
example: A deployment measured at 10 requests/second raw throughput where only 6 of those requests meet TTFT under 2s and ITL under 50ms has a goodput of 6, not 10. Shrinking the maximum batch size from 64 to 32 might drop raw throughput to 9 req/s but raise goodput to 8, because fewer requests now miss their deadlines — a net win for every user even though the headline tokens/second number went down.
tldr: Goodput counts only the requests per second that actually meet their latency SLOs, unlike raw throughput which counts all completions. It aligns capacity planning with user experience.

Teams often measure goodput at average load but the SLO that matters is the one held under peak and bursty traffic. Skip it for pure offline batch jobs where every request shares one loose deadline and raw throughput is the honest number.

faq.q: How is goodput different from throughput?
faq.a: Throughput counts every completed request or token per second; goodput counts only the subset that met their latency SLO. A server can have high throughput and low goodput if large batches push tail latency past the deadline.

faq.q: Why would shrinking batch size raise goodput?
faq.a: Smaller batches lower per-request queuing and decode interference, so more requests stay inside their TTFT and ITL budgets. You trade some raw tokens/second for a higher fraction of requests that actually count.

faq.q: Where did the term come from?
faq.a: It was popularized for LLM serving by the DistServe work on disaggregated prefill and decode, which reported goodput per GPU at fixed SLOs. It is now standard vocabulary in disaggregated-serving discussions.

title: Inter-Token Latency (ITL)
short_definition: The average gap between successive streamed tokens after the first one, also called time per output token (TPOT); it measures how smoothly a response streams during the decode phase.
full_explanation: When a model streams a response, two different waits shape how it feels. The first is the pause before any text appears, captured by time-to-first-token, which reflects prefill. The second is the rhythm of tokens arriving after that, and inter-token latency captures it as the average gap between consecutive output tokens. ITL is what makes a stream feel fluid or stuttery, and it is governed almost entirely by the decode loop rather than the prompt. For a human reading along, a steady ITL in the tens of milliseconds reads as natural typing; for a machine consuming the output, lower is simply faster. Each decode step runs one forward pass that reads the whole KV-cache and produces the next token, and ITL is the wall-clock time of that step averaged across the generation. It grows as batch size grows, because more concurrent requests share memory bandwidth, and it grows as the KV-cache grows with longer contexts, since each step must read more state. End-to-end latency for a response is therefore TTFT plus ITL multiplied by the number of output tokens. Because the distribution has a tail, report both p50 and p99 — a good median with an ugly p99 still produces visible hitches.
why_it_matters: ITL is the difference between a chat that feels alive and one that stutters, and it is the dominant cost term for long outputs since it multiplies by every token generated. For agent and code-generation loops where outputs are consumed by machines, low ITL directly shortens end-to-end task time. It also degrades under exactly the conditions that raise throughput — bigger batches and longer contexts — so it must be watched as load scales.
example: Human reading speed of roughly 10 to 15 tokens/second corresponds to about 70 to 100ms ITL, which feels fluent for chat. A coding agent that consumes a 2,000-token output cares far more: at 100ms ITL the generation alone takes 200 seconds, while at 20ms ITL it takes 40 seconds. If you only watched the median you might miss that p99 ITL doubled under peak load, producing visible pauses for the unlucky tail of requests.
tldr: Inter-token latency is the average time between streamed tokens after the first. It sets how smoothly a response streams and, multiplied by output length, dominates end-to-end latency for long generations.

pitfalls: Quoting only an average ITL hides the p99 spikes that users actually notice, so always report a percentile pair. ITL and TTFT pull in opposite directions under batching — packing more requests improves throughput but worsens both — so tuning one in isolation misleads. People also conflate ITL with tokens-per-second; they are reciprocals only for a single stream, since aggregate tokens/second across a batch can be high while each individual stream's ITL is poor.
when: Track ITL whenever responses stream to a human or feed an agent loop, and use it alongside TTFT to set batch-size and replica limits. You can de-emphasize it for non-streaming batch jobs that only deliver a final result, where total wall-clock per request matters more than per-token smoothness.

faq.q: Is ITL the same as TPOT?
faq.a: Yes. Inter-token latency and time per output token are two names for the same measurement: the average gap between successive output tokens after the first. Some stacks prefer one label over the other.

faq.q: How does ITL relate to TTFT?
faq.a: TTFT is the one-time wait before the first token (prefill); ITL is the recurring gap between every token after it (decode). End-to-end latency is TTFT plus ITL times the number of output tokens.

faq.q: Why does ITL get worse under load?
faq.a: Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so adding concurrent requests to a batch and lengthening contexts both make each step read more KV-cache state, stretching the per-token gap. That is why p99 ITL degrades as a server fills up.

title: Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU)
short_definition: The fraction of a hardware's peak FLOPs a training run spends on the model's defined math: observed tokens/second times theoretical FLOPs per token, over peak hardware FLOPs.
full_explanation: Peak hardware FLOPs is a sticker number no real workload reaches, so comparing training stacks by raw GPU count or wall-clock is unfair. MFU normalizes this: it asks what fraction of the chip's theoretical peak is going into the FLOPs the model definition actually requires, ignoring everything the implementation wastes. Introduced in the PaLM report, it became the standard way to compare how efficiently different stacks use the same silicon. A run at 40% MFU is leaving more than half the chip idle to communication, memory stalls, and kernel overhead — and knowing that points you at where to optimize. You compute the theoretical FLOPs per token from the model's parameter count and sequence length (a common approximation is roughly six times the parameter count per token for a dense transformer's forward plus backward pass), multiply by observed tokens per second to get achieved FLOPs, and divide by the hardware's advertised peak for the relevant dtype. Crucially, MFU counts only the model-defined math as useful, so activation recomputation does not help your score. That is the key contrast with hardware FLOPs utilization, which credits recomputation as real work; because HFU counts those extra FLOPs, HFU is always at least as large as MFU. Decode-phase inference is memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound, so very low MFU there is expected and not a defect.
why_it_matters: MFU turns a vague sense that training is slow into a single comparable efficiency number, and the gap between your MFU and the well-tuned ceiling is a direct budget for optimization. It lets teams compare stacks across different cluster sizes fairly and decide whether to invest in better kernels, communication overlap, or parallelism layout. Misreading it — for instance expecting training-like MFU during decode — wastes effort chasing a number that is supposed to be low.
example: Well-tuned large-scale LLM training typically lands somewhere around 30 to 50% MFU; the remaining half-plus is lost to inter-GPU communication, memory-bandwidth stalls, and kernel launch overhead. If a stack reports 35% MFU but its HFU is 55%, the 20-point gap is the cost of activation checkpointing — recomputed FLOPs that HFU counts as work but MFU correctly excludes, since they do not advance the model's defined computation.
tldr: MFU is the fraction of peak hardware FLOPs a training run spends on the model's defined math. Large LLM runs hit roughly 30 to 50%; the rest is overhead.

Avoid treating it as the figure of merit for the decode phase of inference, where memory-bandwidth metrics describe the bottleneck far better.

faq.q: What MFU should I expect for LLM training?
faq.a: Well-optimized large-scale runs commonly sit around 30 to 50% MFU. Lower than that usually points at communication overhead, memory stalls, or unoptimized kernels rather than a hardware limit.

faq.q: How is MFU different from HFU?

faq.q: Why is MFU so low during inference decode?
faq.a: Decode generates one token at a time and is bottlenecked by reading the KV-cache from memory, not by arithmetic. That makes it memory-bandwidth-bound, so low MFU during decode is expected rather than a sign of a problem.

title: SmoothQuant
short_definition: A post-training W8A8 quantization method that migrates quantization difficulty from activations into weights via a per-channel scale, enabling full INT8 matrix multiplies with minimal accuracy loss.
full_explanation: Quantizing LLM weights to INT8 is easy; quantizing activations is where things break. The reason is a handful of activation channels carry outlier values orders of magnitude larger than the rest, and a single per-tensor INT8 scale forced to span those outliers crushes the precision of everything else, wrecking accuracy. Weight-only methods dodge this by leaving activations in fp16, but then the matrix multiplies still run in fp16 and you lose the compute speedup. SmoothQuant, from Xiao and colleagues at MIT and NVIDIA, takes a different route: it mathematically rebalances the problem so both sides become INT8-friendly. The trick rests on the fact that for a linear layer, dividing the activations by a per-channel factor and multiplying the corresponding weight columns by the same factor leaves the product unchanged. SmoothQuant chooses that per-channel scale to pull the outlier magnitude out of the activations and push it into the weights, which tolerate it well, using a scale of the form s_j equal to max absolute activation in channel j raised to alpha over max absolute weight raised to one minus alpha, with alpha around 0.5 balancing the migration. After this equivalent transform, a standard per-tensor or per-channel INT8 quantizer handles both tensors cleanly. The payoff is genuine INT8 GEMMs for weights and activations together, which delivers real latency gains rather than just memory savings.
why_it_matters: Activation outliers are the single reason naive INT8 fails on transformers, and SmoothQuant is the technique that made W8A8 practical without retraining. Because both operands are INT8, you get actual compute acceleration on INT8 tensor cores, not just the bandwidth relief of weight-only schemes. It shipped in production serving stacks, so it is a default tool when you need INT8 throughput on hardware tuned for it.
example: On large OPT and BLOOM-class models, SmoothQuant reaches full INT8 weight-and-activation GEMMs with accuracy close to the fp16 baseline and latency improvements in the roughly 1.5x class, unlike weight-only INT8 which still computes in fp16 and so leaves that speedup on the table. The method is exposed in TensorRT-LLM and vLLM quantization paths, where you supply calibration data and it computes the per-channel migration scales offline.
tldr: SmoothQuant shifts activation outliers into the weights via an equivalent per-channel rescale, so both go to INT8. The result is full W8A8 matmuls with real latency gains.

Calibration data must resemble real inputs, since the per-channel scales are estimated from observed activation ranges. And SmoothQuant targets INT8; it is not the same lever as the 4-bit weight-only methods, so do not expect 4-bit memory footprints from it.

Prefer weight-only 4-bit methods instead when the goal is to shrink memory footprint to fit a model on a smaller GPU and you do not need INT8 activation math.

faq.q: Why can't you just quantize activations to INT8 directly?
faq.a: LLM activations contain outlier channels far larger than the rest. A single INT8 scale stretched to cover those outliers destroys precision on the normal channels, so naive activation quantization loses significant accuracy.

faq.q: How does SmoothQuant differ from weight-only methods like AWQ or GPTQ?
faq.a: AWQ and GPTQ quantize weights only and run activations in fp16, so the GEMM stays fp16. SmoothQuant quantizes both weights and activations to INT8, giving actual INT8 compute speedups in addition to memory savings.

faq.q: Does SmoothQuant require retraining?
faq.a: No. It is post-training: you run a calibration pass to estimate per-channel ranges, compute the migration scales, and fold them in. No gradient updates to the model are needed.

title: MXFP4 (Microscaling FP4)
short_definition: A 4-bit float from the OCP Microscaling spec where a 32-element block shares one 8-bit power-of-two scale and each element is FP4 E2M1, about 4.25 bits per value with per-block range.
full_explanation: Plain 4-bit floating point has almost no dynamic range, so a single global scale either clips the large values or starves the small ones. The Microscaling family fixes this by attaching scales at fine block granularity instead of per-tensor. MXFP4, defined in the OCP Microscaling specification backed by a consortium of major silicon and software vendors, groups elements into blocks of 32 that share one 8-bit power-of-two scale in E8M0 format, while each individual element is stored as FP4 in E2M1. The shared exponent amortizes to a small per-element overhead, so the effective cost is about 4.25 bits per value, and because every block gets its own scale, local outliers are absorbed far better than a flat FP4 quantizer could. Mechanically, you partition each weight tensor into contiguous 32-element blocks, pick the block's E8M0 scale from its maximum magnitude, and quantize each element to the nearest E2M1 value after dividing by that scale; at compute time the scale is reapplied. NVFP4 is the Blackwell-era sibling that uses 16-element blocks and FP8 E4M3 scales together with hardware-accelerated FP4 tensor cores. The practical caveat is that block formats handle outliers better than plain FP4 but are not magic: the most sensitive layers, often the first and last layers and parts of attention, are commonly kept at higher precision.
why_it_matters: Four-bit weights roughly halve memory versus 8-bit and quarter it versus fp16, which is the difference between a model fitting on one GPU or needing several. Block scaling is what makes 4-bit floating point accurate enough to use for real weights rather than a research curiosity. With Blackwell-class hardware accelerating FP4 directly, these formats also turn the memory saving into compute throughput, not just a smaller footprint.
example: OpenAI's gpt-oss release shipped its mixture-of-experts weights in MXFP4, which let the 120B-parameter model run on a single 80GB GPU — a footprint that would be impossible at fp16. NVFP4, NVIDIA's variant, pairs 16-element blocks with FP8 E4M3 scales and FP4 tensor cores on Blackwell so the 4-bit weights are also multiplied in hardware. In both, sensitive layers such as the first and last are typically left at higher precision to protect quality.
tldr: MXFP4 is an OCP 4-bit float where 32 elements share an 8-bit scale. Block scaling absorbs outliers, letting large MoE models like gpt-oss fit on a single 80GB GPU.

Quality is uneven across layers — applying MXFP4 uniformly, including to the most sensitive layers, tends to hurt, so mixed precision is the norm. MXFP4 and NVFP4 differ in block size and scale format and are not interchangeable bit layouts, so target the format your hardware actually accelerates.

On Blackwell-class hardware prefer the variant with native FP4 tensor-core support so the 4-bit weights also accelerate compute rather than only shrinking memory.

faq.q: Why is MXFP4 'about 4.25 bits' rather than exactly 4?
faq.a: Each value is 4 bits (FP4 E2M1), but every block of 32 elements also stores one shared 8-bit scale. Spreading that 8-bit scale across 32 values adds roughly a quarter of a bit per element.

faq.q: How is NVFP4 different from MXFP4?
faq.a: NVFP4 is NVIDIA's Blackwell-era variant using 16-element blocks and FP8 E4M3 scales, with hardware-accelerated FP4 tensor cores. MXFP4 uses 32-element blocks and 8-bit power-of-two (E8M0) scales per the OCP spec.

faq.q: Can every layer be quantized to MXFP4 safely?
faq.a: Not reliably. Block scaling handles outliers better than flat FP4, but sensitive layers — often the first, last, and parts of attention — are commonly kept at higher precision to preserve accuracy.

title: Batch Invariance
short_definition: The property that a request's output does not depend on which other requests share its batch; standard kernels lack it, a root cause of nondeterminism even at temperature zero.
full_explanation: Most people assume an LLM at temperature zero is deterministic, then are surprised when identical inputs produce different outputs run to run. A major culprit is that standard inference kernels are not batch-invariant. The reduction order and tiling strategy inside a matmul or normalization change depending on the batch size and shape, and because floating-point addition is not associative, summing the same numbers in a different order yields slightly different bits. Those tiny differences in the logits can flip an argmax, so the very same prompt can decode differently solely because of which other requests it was batched with at that moment. Batch invariance is the property of kernels that produce identical results for a request regardless of its batch neighbors. Achieving it means writing the reduction-bearing operations — RMSNorm, matmul, attention — so their accumulation order is fixed and independent of batch dimensions, rather than letting the library pick whatever tiling is fastest for the current shape. Thinking Machines' work on defeating nondeterminism in LLM inference built exactly these batch-invariant kernels and reported bitwise-reproducible inference at a modest throughput cost. The reason to pay that cost is concrete: reproducible evaluations, debuggable failures, and truly on-policy reinforcement learning where the sampler's numerics match the trainer's.
why_it_matters: Nondeterminism at temperature zero quietly undermines trust — bug reports that will not reproduce, evals that drift between runs, and A/B comparisons muddied by numerical noise. Batch invariance is the missing property that makes inference bitwise-reproducible, which matters most for science-grade evaluation and debugging. It also tightens reinforcement-learning loops, because on-policy methods assume the samples were drawn from the policy you are updating, and mismatched sampler-versus-trainer numerics violate that assumption.
example: Thinking Machines' 'Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference' built batch-invariant RMSNorm, matmul, and attention kernels and demonstrated bitwise-identical outputs for the same prompt regardless of concurrent batch composition, at a modest throughput cost. Concretely, before the fix, sending one prompt alone versus sending it inside a batch of 32 could yield different completions at temperature zero; after, the two paths produce the same tokens because the reductions accumulate in a fixed order.
tldr: Batch invariance means a request decodes the same regardless of who shares its batch. Standard kernels lack it because batch-dependent reduction order plus float non-associativity perturbs logits, causing temperature-zero nondeterminism.

Batch-invariant kernels cost some throughput, so it is a deliberate tradeoff rather than a free default. Determinism is also fragile across the rest of the stack: changing hardware, library versions, or parallelism layout can reintroduce variation even with batch-invariant kernels, so reproducibility claims must pin the whole environment.

Skip them in throughput-first production serving that tolerates run-to-run numerical noise, since they trade some speed for the reproducibility you do not need there.

faq.q: Why isn't temperature zero already deterministic?
faq.a: Temperature zero only fixes the sampling rule to argmax; it does not fix the logits. Batch-dependent reduction order combined with floating-point non-associativity perturbs the logits enough to flip the argmax, so outputs still vary.

faq.q: What does batch invariance cost?
faq.a: Fixing reduction order forgoes some shape-specific kernel optimizations, so throughput drops modestly. The reported tradeoff is bitwise reproducibility in exchange for a moderate reduction in serving speed.

faq.q: Where does batch invariance matter most?
faq.a: Reproducible evaluation and debugging, and on-policy reinforcement learning. In RL the sampler must match the trainer's numerics so samples are genuinely on-policy; batch-variant kernels break that alignment.

title: RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards)
short_definition: Reinforcement-learning post-training where the reward comes from a programmatic verifier — tests passing, a math answer matching, a format holding — instead of a learned reward model.
full_explanation: Standard RLHF trains a reward model to imitate human preferences, then optimizes against it, which works but invites reward hacking: the policy learns to exploit the reward model's blind spots rather than genuinely improve. RLVR sidesteps that whole failure class in domains where correctness is checkable. Instead of a learned scorer, the reward is a deterministic verifier — the unit tests pass or they do not, the final answer equals the reference integer or it does not, the output matches the required format or it does not. Because the verifier is ground truth, there is no proxy to game. The term was coined in AI2's Tulu 3 work, and DeepSeek-R1 made the recipe widely known by showing that large-scale RL with simple rule-based rewards can elicit long, emergent chains of thought. You roll out completions from the current policy, run each through the verifier to assign a scalar reward (often just pass or fail), and update the policy to make rewarded behaviors more likely, commonly with GRPO as the optimizer. The catch is scope: RLVR only applies where a cheap, reliable checker exists — math, code, formal constraints — and whether the gains generalize to fuzzy open-ended tasks is the open research question.
why_it_matters: Reward hacking is the central headache of preference-model RL, and RLVR removes it outright wherever a verifier exists, which is why it underlies recent jumps on math and coding benchmarks. It also makes the reward cheap and reproducible — running tests costs far less than maintaining a reward model — and the signal is unambiguous. The limitation is equally important: it shapes capability investment toward checkable domains, so teams must decide where verifiable rewards stop and learned preferences must take over.

AI2's Tulu 3, which coined the RLVR term, applied verifiable rewards across tasks like math and instruction-following where outputs can be checked against a rule. In both, GRPO is a common optimizer pairing because it estimates advantages from groups of sampled completions without a separate value network.
tldr: RLVR rewards a model from a programmatic verifier — tests pass, the answer matches — not a learned reward model. It avoids reward hacking but only covers checkable domains.

faq.a: Tasks with cheap, reliable checkers: math problems with exact answers, code judged by unit tests, and outputs that must satisfy a format constraint. Open-ended generation without a clean verifier is a poor fit.

title: Muon Optimizer
short_definition: An optimizer for 2D weight matrices that orthogonalizes the SGD-momentum update with a few Newton-Schulz iterations before applying it, born in NanoGPT speedruns and later scaled up.
full_explanation: AdamW treats every parameter as an independent scalar and rescales it by its own running gradient statistics, which ignores that a weight matrix has structure. Muon — short for MomentUm Orthogonalized by Newton-Schulz — exploits that structure for 2D matrices. The intuition is that a good update to a matrix should not collapse its directions onto a few dominant ones; orthogonalizing the update spreads the step across directions more evenly, which empirically trains faster. Keller Jordan introduced it in the context of NanoGPT speedruns, where shaving wall-clock to a target loss is the whole game, and it then proved to scale. For a 2D weight matrix, Muon takes the usual SGD-with-momentum update and then orthogonalizes it: roughly five Newton-Schulz iterations approximate the nearest semi-orthogonal matrix to the raw update, and that orthogonalized version is what gets applied. Parameters without useful 2D matrix structure — embeddings, normalization scales, scalar biases — stay on AdamW, so Muon is used as a targeted replacement rather than a wholesale one. At scale, Moonshot's Moonlight reported on the order of twice the computational efficiency of AdamW at their setting, and Kimi K2, a trillion-parameter model, trained with MuonClip — Muon plus a QK-clip mechanism that caps attention-logit growth — reporting no loss spikes across 15.5 trillion tokens.
why_it_matters: Optimizer efficiency translates directly into training cost, so an update rule that reaches the same loss in fewer steps is real money at frontier scale. Muon's reported efficiency edge over AdamW, and its demonstrated stability at trillion-parameter scale with MuonClip, make it one of the few credible challengers to AdamW's long dominance. The QK-clip pairing also addresses attention-logit blowups, a recurring source of training instability, which matters as much as raw speed when a single run costs a fortune.

Kimi K2, a trillion-parameter model, trained with MuonClip — Muon plus QK-clip to stop attention-logit blowups — and reported zero loss spikes across 15.5 trillion tokens. In a typical setup the 2D transformer weight matrices run on Muon while embeddings, norms, and scalar parameters stay on AdamW.
tldr: Muon orthogonalizes the momentum update for 2D weight matrices via Newton-Schulz, keeping embeddings on AdamW. It reported about 2x efficiency at scale; MuonClip adds logit clipping.

title: Sequence Packing
short_definition: Concatenating short training examples into one fixed-length row so padding stops wasting compute, with attention masking and position-id resets so packed examples do not attend across boundaries.
full_explanation: Training batches use fixed-length rows, but real examples vary in length, so the usual fix is to pad every example up to the maximum. When a dataset skews short — instruction-tuning data often does — that padding can be most of the tensor, and the GPU spends its time multiplying zeros. Sequence packing removes the waste by concatenating several short examples end to end into one full-length row, so almost every position carries real tokens. The subtlety is that a naive concatenation lets one example attend to the tokens of another, leaking information across documents that should be independent. Proper packing prevents that with a block-diagonal attention mask (or FlashAttention variable-length kernels) so each example only attends within its own span, plus per-example position-id resets so positions restart at each boundary rather than counting across the whole row. Because SFT datasets are heavy on short samples, packing commonly yields a 2 to 4x throughput improvement. The dangerous part is that the bug hides: if you forget the masking, models still mostly train fine because cross-contamination is a weak signal, so the throughput win looks free while a subtle correctness problem rides along. It is built into tools like axolotl and TRL under the name sample packing.
why_it_matters: Padding waste is pure lost compute, and on short-skewed datasets it can dominate the batch, so packing is among the cheapest large throughput wins in fine-tuning. The catch is that the masking is easy to get subtly wrong, and because an unmasked model still appears to train, the mistake can ship silently and quietly degrade quality. Knowing that packing requires both block-diagonal masking and position resets is what separates a correct 2 to 4x speedup from a quiet bug.
example: An SFT dataset where the average example is 200 tokens but the row length is 2,048 wastes most of each row on padding; packing roughly ten such examples per row pushes utilization up and commonly gives a 2 to 4x throughput improvement. Done correctly, a block-diagonal mask keeps example three from attending to example two, and position ids reset to zero at each example's start. Tools such as axolotl and TRL expose this as sample packing so you do not implement the masking by hand.
tldr: Sequence packing concatenates short examples into one full row to kill padding waste, using block-diagonal masks and position resets so examples stay independent. Commonly a 2 to 4x SFT gain.

faq.a: Examples in the same row attend across boundaries and leak information between unrelated documents. The model usually still trains, so the bug hides — you get the speedup with a subtle, silent correctness problem.

title: Mid-Training
short_definition: A loosely defined phase between pretraining and post-training where a model anneals on high-quality and instructional data, extends context, and infuses domain data, usually during LR decay.
full_explanation: The clean story of pretrain-then-finetune hides a messy and consequential middle. After the bulk of next-token pretraining on a broad corpus, labs run a phase — increasingly called mid-training — that anneals the model on a curated mixture: higher-quality web text, instructional data, more code and math, often while extending the context window, and typically overlapping the learning-rate decay. It is still next-token prediction on corpora, which distinguishes it from supervised fine-tuning on chat templates; the model is not yet being taught to follow an assistant format, it is being steered by what it reads as the learning rate winds down. The term spread through 2024 and 2025 model reports, with OLMo 2's mid-training stage being the canonical public writeup and Phi and others describing equivalents. Mechanically, you take a checkpoint from the stable pretraining phase and continue training on the curated mixture while decaying the learning rate, so the data the model sees during decay carries outsized weight in shaping the final result. This is where a lot of capability quietly appears, because the decay-phase mixture disproportionately determines what the finished base model is good at — which is also why labs are often vague about exactly what goes into it.
why_it_matters: Mid-training is where much of a base model's measured capability is actually decided, yet it is the least standardized and least documented part of the pipeline. Because the decay-phase data mixture has outsized influence on the final model, decisions made here drive benchmark differences that look like architecture or scale wins but are really data-curation wins. Understanding it reframes how you read model reports: a strong base model may owe its edge to its mid-training mixture more than to its pretraining corpus.
example: OLMo 2 documented a distinct mid-training stage — annealing on a high-quality and instruction-heavy mixture during learning-rate decay — as the canonical public description of the phase, and Phi-family models describe analogous curated late-stage training. In practice a team might branch from a stable pretraining checkpoint, then spend the decay phase on a mixture weighted toward math, code, and cleaner text plus longer contexts, and find the resulting base model markedly stronger on reasoning benchmarks than the pre-decay checkpoint despite no architecture change.
tldr: Mid-training is the curated phase between pretraining and post-training: anneal on high-quality, instructional, and domain data during LR decay. Still next-token prediction; shapes much of capability.

The concept matters less if you only consume already-finished open-weight models, where the mid-training choices are baked in and not yours to set.

faq.a: Mid-training is still next-token prediction on corpora, just on a curated late-stage mixture during LR decay. SFT trains on chat-formatted instruction-response pairs to shape assistant behavior. They are different stages with different objectives.

faq.q: Why does the decay-phase data matter so much?
faq.a: As the learning rate decays, the model's parameters settle, so data seen during decay disproportionately shapes the final weights. A curated mixture here can drive large benchmark gains without any architecture change.

title: WSD Schedule (Warmup-Stable-Decay)
short_definition: A learning-rate schedule with a warmup, a long flat plateau at the peak rate, then a short sharp decay over the final fraction of steps, so you need not fix a total step count up front.
full_explanation: Cosine learning-rate schedules have a hidden constraint: you must know the total number of steps up front, because the curve is shaped to reach its minimum exactly at the end. That makes continual pretraining and data ablations awkward — extend the run and the schedule no longer fits. The Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule, popularized by MiniCPM and also called trapezoidal, removes that constraint. After a warmup it holds the learning rate flat at its peak for a long stable plateau, then applies a short sharp decay only over roughly the final 10 to 20% of steps. Because the plateau does not encode a horizon, you can branch from any plateau checkpoint and run just the short decay to produce a finished model, which makes checkpoint reuse, continual pretraining, and data-mixture ablations cheap. Operationally you keep one long stable run going, and whenever you want a deliverable model at some token budget, you fork the latest plateau checkpoint and apply the decay. The notable empirical property is that most of the final quality materializes during that decay phase — the plateau checkpoint looks mediocre and then improves sharply as the rate drops. The corresponding pitfall follows directly: comparing plateau-phase checkpoints across runs understates their true post-decay quality.
why_it_matters: Committing to a total step count is a real planning cost, and WSD removes it, which is why it underpins workflows built around continual pretraining and cheap ablations. One long stable run can spawn many finished models at different budgets by paying only the short decay each time, instead of rerunning a fresh cosine schedule per target. The flip side is an evaluation trap: plateau checkpoints look worse than they will become, so naive mid-run comparisons mislead unless you decay first.
example: MiniCPM popularized WSD: a warmup, a long flat plateau, then a sharp decay over the final fraction of steps. A team running one stable plateau can fork the checkpoint at, say, 1T tokens and at 1.5T tokens, run the short decay on each, and get two finished models from a single long run without committing to either budget in advance. Because quality jumps during decay, the 1T plateau checkpoint evaluated before its decay would badly understate the model it becomes after decaying.
tldr: WSD warms up, holds the rate flat for a long plateau, then decays sharply at the end. Branch any plateau checkpoint and decay it, enabling continual pretraining and ablations.

WSD also interacts with the data mixture during decay (the same window mid-training exploits), so changing both at once muddies what caused a result.
when: Choose WSD when you want to avoid committing to a total step count, run continual pretraining, or fork one long run into several finished models at different budgets. Stick with a cosine schedule for a single run with a fixed, known token budget where its smooth decay is well understood and the branching flexibility is unnecessary.

faq.a: Cosine requires committing to a total step count, since the curve targets its minimum at the end. WSD holds a long flat plateau then decays over the final fraction, so you can branch any plateau checkpoint and decay it without a preset horizon.

faq.a: Most of the final quality materializes during the short decay phase. A checkpoint taken on the plateau, before decay, understates the model's post-decay performance, which can mislead mid-run comparisons.

faq.q: What is WSD good for in practice?
faq.a: Continual pretraining, data-mixture ablations, and producing several finished models at different token budgets from one long run — each by forking a plateau checkpoint and paying only the short decay.

title: Expert Parallelism
short_definition: A parallelism strategy for mixture-of-experts that shards experts across devices and routes each token via all-to-all to the device holding its selected experts, then gathers results back.
full_explanation: A mixture-of-experts layer has far more parameters than any single device can hold, but each token only uses a few experts, so replicating all experts everywhere is wasteful. Expert parallelism shards the experts across devices instead: each device stores a subset of the experts. Because the router sends different tokens to different experts, a token's hidden state often needs to travel to a device other than the one it started on. This is done with all-to-all communication — every device simultaneously exchanges the tokens destined for experts elsewhere — after which each device runs its local experts and a second all-to-all gathers the outputs back to where the tokens belong. Expert parallelism composes with data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism, so it is one axis in a larger parallelization plan. The defining problem is load imbalance: routing is data-dependent, so some experts get far more tokens than others, and those hot experts become stragglers that stall the all-to-all. Mitigations include capacity factors that cap tokens per expert, auxiliary balance losses that push the router toward even assignment, and DeepSeek-V3's bias-based aux-loss-free balancing; V3 also restricts each token's experts to a small number of nodes to bound the all-to-all cost. The same machinery is used at inference, for example with DeepSeek's DeepEP communication kernels.
why_it_matters: MoE models are how labs scale parameter count without scaling per-token compute, and expert parallelism is the layout that makes those parameters fit across a cluster. Its bottleneck is all-to-all communication and the stragglers that load imbalance creates, so balancing strategy is as important to throughput as raw compute. The techniques that fix it — capacity factors, balance losses, aux-loss-free schemes — are central to training and serving large MoE models efficiently.
example: DeepSeek-V3 shards its many experts with expert parallelism and uses bias-based aux-loss-free load balancing to keep experts evenly used, while restricting each token to experts on a few nodes so the all-to-all stays bounded. At inference, DeepSeek's DeepEP kernels implement the expert all-to-all efficiently. A simpler illustration: with 64 experts sharded across 8 devices, each device holds 8 experts, and every layer performs two all-to-all exchanges — one to dispatch tokens to their experts and one to return the outputs.
tldr: Expert parallelism shards MoE experts across devices and routes each token to its experts via all-to-all. Load imbalance from hot experts is the core problem, fixed with balancing schemes.

faq.a: MoE experts hold far more parameters than one device can store, so replication is infeasible. Sharding experts and using all-to-all to send each token to its chosen experts keeps the memory footprint per device manageable.

faq.a: No. It is used at inference too — for example DeepSeek's DeepEP kernels implement the expert all-to-all efficiently for serving large MoE models, not just for training them.

title: Native Sparse Attention (NSA)
short_definition: DeepSeek's sparse attention that is trainable end-to-end and hardware-aligned, blending compressed coarse tokens, selected fine-grained blocks, and a sliding window per query, not applied post-hoc.
full_explanation: Most sparse-attention schemes are bolted on after a model is trained dense, dropping attention connections at inference to save long-context cost — and they tend to degrade quality, because the model never learned to work with the sparsity. DeepSeek's Native Sparse Attention takes the opposite stance: make the sparsity part of training so the model adapts to it, and design it to match hardware so the theoretical savings are real. For each query it runs three parallel branches. One attends to compressed, coarse-grained representations of distant context to keep a cheap global view; a second selects a small number of fine-grained token blocks, the top-n most relevant, to preserve detail where it matters; and a third is a sliding window over recent tokens for local continuity. Learned gates combine the three branches, and the whole thing is blockwise so its memory-access pattern aligns with tensor-core granularity rather than fighting it. Because the model trains natively sparse, it keeps quality that post-hoc sparsification loses, while cutting long-context cost in both prefill and decode. Production sparse attention in DeepSeek's later releases descends from this line of work.
why_it_matters: Long-context attention is expensive in both compute and KV-cache, and post-hoc sparsity buys speed at the price of quality. NSA's contribution is showing that training the sparsity in keeps quality while delivering the savings, and that hardware-aligned block design turns those savings into real wall-clock gains rather than theoretical FLOP reductions. That it speeds up both prefill and decode, not just one phase, makes it relevant to the full long-context serving cost.
example: For a long document, NSA gives each query a cheap global view through compressed coarse tokens, sharp detail through a handful of selected fine-grained blocks (top-n selection), and local continuity through a sliding window, with learned gates blending the three. Because the model is trained with this structure rather than having it imposed at inference, it retains quality that a model trained dense and sparsified afterward would lose. DeepSeek's later production sparse-attention releases build on this approach.
tldr: NSA is DeepSeek's trainable, hardware-aligned sparse attention: per query it blends compressed coarse tokens, selected fine-grained blocks, and a sliding window. Training sparse keeps quality.

title: Tree Attention
short_definition: An attention masking scheme that verifies a tree of speculative candidate continuations in one forward pass: flatten the tree, mask so each node attends only to its ancestors.
full_explanation: Speculative decoding proposes draft tokens that the target model then verifies; the speedup grows if you can verify many candidate continuations at once instead of a single path. Tree attention is the mechanism that makes that possible. Multiple draft branches form a tree — different possible next tokens, and different possible tokens after each of those — and instead of checking each path separately, the tree is flattened into one sequence and fed through the model in a single forward pass. The trick is the mask: a topology-aware attention mask lets each node attend only to its own ancestors in the tree, so every candidate path sees exactly the prefix it should and no sibling leakage occurs. Concretely you lay the tree's nodes out in one row, build the mask from the parent-child structure, run one forward pass, and then accept the longest path whose tokens the target model agrees with. This is what speculative systems like SpecInfer, Medusa, and EAGLE-2's dynamic trees use to score many branches simultaneously rather than one at a time. The cost is not free, though: it grows with the tree size, so beyond a few dozen nodes the extra branches stop paying for themselves and a bigger tree slows things down instead of speeding them up.
why_it_matters: Verifying a tree instead of a single draft path is what lets speculative decoding accept more tokens per forward pass, directly improving decode speed. Tree attention is the masking primitive every modern tree-based speculative system depends on, so understanding it explains how Medusa, EAGLE-2, and SpecInfer get their gains. It also has a clear cost ceiling — tree size has diminishing returns — which is essential for tuning these systems rather than naively enlarging the tree.
example: EAGLE-2 builds dynamic candidate trees and verifies them with a topology-aware mask in one forward pass, accepting the longest path the target model confirms; Medusa's parallel heads and SpecInfer similarly rely on tree attention to score multiple branches at once. If a tree has, say, 32 nodes spread across several branches, the model still does one forward pass over the flattened 32-token sequence, and the mask ensures each leaf only attended to its own root-to-leaf prefix. Push the tree past a few dozen nodes and the per-pass cost outweighs the extra acceptance.
tldr: Tree attention verifies a tree of speculative draft branches in one forward pass: flatten it, mask so each node attends only to its ancestors, and accept the longest confirmed path.

It is irrelevant outside speculative decoding — for plain single-path decoding there is no tree to verify, so the masking machinery adds nothing.

faq.a: Checking many candidate continuations in a single forward pass raises the chance of accepting a longer run of tokens per step, which improves decode speed more than verifying one path at a time.

faq.a: It is topology-aware: each node attends only to its ancestors in the tree. That guarantees every candidate path sees exactly its own prefix, with no leakage between sibling branches, even though all nodes share one flattened sequence.

title: Byte Latent Transformer (BLT)
short_definition: Meta's tokenizer-free architecture that groups raw bytes into dynamic patches sized by next-byte entropy, runs the main transformer over patch latents, and decodes back to bytes.
full_explanation: Tokenizers cause a long list of headaches — unfair compression across languages, glitch tokens, blindness to character-level structure — because they impose a fixed vocabulary learned on one corpus. The Byte Latent Transformer removes the tokenizer entirely and operates on raw bytes, but it avoids the naive cost of byte-level modeling by grouping bytes into variable-length patches. The key idea is that not all bytes are equally hard to predict: a small byte-level language model estimates next-byte entropy, and patch boundaries are drawn where entropy is high, so easy, predictable spans become long patches and hard, surprising spans become short ones. A lightweight local encoder maps the bytes in each patch to a patch latent, the main transformer — the bulk of the compute — runs over the sequence of patch latents, and a local decoder turns latents back into bytes. Because patch size is dynamic, this also opens a new scaling axis: grow the average patch size and you spend more of the budget on the latent transformer per byte processed. At the 8B scale, BLT matched tokenizer-based peers while being more robust to spelling and noise, and it directly addresses tokenizer pathologies like multilingual unfairness, glitch tokens, and character-level blindness.
why_it_matters: Tokenizers are a quiet source of real problems — some languages pay several times more tokens per word, glitch tokens destabilize outputs, and models struggle with character-level tasks — and BLT attacks the root by dropping the tokenizer. Matching tokenizer-based peers at 8B scale while improving robustness to spelling and noise shows the approach is competitive, not just a curiosity. The dynamic-patch scaling axis is also a different lever than parameters or data, which is interesting for how future models trade compute.
example: BLT decides boundaries with a small byte-level entropy model: the predictable run 'the ' might become one long patch while a rare proper noun or a typo fragments into short patches, so compute concentrates where bytes are hard to predict. At 8B parameters it matched tokenizer-based models of comparable scale on standard tasks while handling misspellings and noisy input more gracefully, because nothing depends on a fixed vocabulary. Growing the average patch size shifts more compute into the main transformer per byte, a knob tokenizer-based models do not have.
tldr: BLT is Meta's tokenizer-free model: a small entropy model splits bytes into dynamic patches, the transformer runs over patch latents, a decoder emits bytes. At 8B it matched tokenizer-based peers.

The patching is dynamic, which complicates batching and serving compared with fixed tokens. And while it matched tokenizer-based peers at 8B, that does not by itself prove the advantage holds at every scale or task, so it remains a developing approach rather than a settled default.

Stick with established tokenizer-based models when you need a mature, well-supported serving stack and tokenizer issues are not a primary concern.

title: Diffusion Language Model
short_definition: A text generator that produces output by iterative parallel denoising — mask-and-refill updating many tokens per step — instead of left-to-right autoregression one token at a time.
full_explanation: Autoregressive language models generate strictly left to right, one token per forward pass, which is simple and high-quality but inherently sequential. Diffusion language models borrow the denoising idea from image diffusion and apply it to text: start from a heavily masked or noised sequence and iteratively refine it, filling in and revising many tokens in parallel at each step rather than committing to one token at a time. Because each step can update many positions at once, the headline win is speed in the right regimes. The model has bidirectional context — it can see both sides of a position while denoising — which makes it a natural fit for infilling and edit-style tasks where the surrounding text is known. Operationally, you run a fixed or adaptive number of denoising steps, and the number of steps is a direct quality-versus-speed dial: fewer steps generate faster but can sacrifice quality, more steps approach the model's best output. LLaDA was the first open competitive diffusion LM at 8B scale; Inception Labs' Mercury and Google's Gemini Diffusion demonstrated the speed story, with reports of substantially faster decode where the regime suits it. The tradeoffs are real: quality-per-FLOP at the frontier still favors autoregression, KV-cache reuse and exact streaming semantics are harder, and the step count must be tuned.
why_it_matters: Decode speed is a core serving cost, and updating many tokens per step is a structurally different way to attack it than speculative decoding on an autoregressive model. The bidirectional nature also makes diffusion LMs a strong fit for infilling and editing, where autoregression's left-to-right constraint is awkward. At the same time the honest tradeoffs — frontier quality-per-FLOP still favoring AR, harder caching and streaming — matter for deciding where the approach actually pays off versus where it does not.
example: LLaDA was the first open competitive diffusion language model at 8B scale, and Inception Labs' Mercury and Google's Gemini Diffusion showed the headline result: updating many tokens per denoising step gives much faster decode in the right regimes than token-by-token autoregression. For an infilling task — completing the middle of a code block with both sides fixed — a diffusion LM uses its bidirectional context naturally, whereas an autoregressive model must work around its left-to-right constraint. The number of denoising steps trades quality against speed directly.
tldr: A diffusion LM generates text by iterative parallel denoising, updating many tokens per step. It can decode much faster in good regimes and suits infilling, but frontier quality favors AR.

Prefer autoregressive models for frontier-quality open-ended generation and when you need mature KV-cache reuse and exact token-by-token streaming.

title: Hybrid SSM-Transformer
short_definition: An architecture interleaving state-space (Mamba-style) layers with a minority of attention layers, getting cheap long-sequence throughput from SSM layers and precise retrieval from attention layers.
full_explanation: Pure attention scales poorly with sequence length and its KV-cache grows without bound, while pure state-space models are cheap on long sequences but weak at precise retrieval and in-context learning. Hybrid SSM-Transformer architectures take the pragmatic middle: mostly state-space layers, with a minority of attention layers sprinkled in. The state-space layers carry a constant-size recurrent state instead of a growing KV-cache, so they handle long sequences cheaply and with high throughput; the few attention layers restore the exact token-to-token lookup and in-context learning that SSMs struggle to do alone. Jamba from AI21 used roughly a 1-to-7 ratio of attention to Mamba layers, and Nemotron-H, Zamba, and IBM's Granite 4 follow the same pattern. The result is large reductions in KV-cache memory and strong long-context throughput at quality close to a pure-attention model of similar size, because the handful of attention layers cover the cases SSMs are weak on. The catch is maturity: hybrid inference stacks are younger than transformer stacks, so paged attention, prefix caching, and speculative tricks need SSM-aware reworking before they apply cleanly.
why_it_matters: KV-cache growth is a primary cost and memory limiter for long-context transformers, and replacing most layers with constant-state SSM layers cuts that dramatically while keeping near-parity quality. The few retained attention layers are what preserve precise retrieval and in-context learning, so the hybrid avoids the weakness that kept pure SSMs from displacing transformers. The practical caveat — younger inference tooling — matters for anyone planning to deploy, since familiar serving optimizations may not work out of the box.
example: Jamba interleaved attention and Mamba layers at about a 1-to-7 ratio, and Nemotron-H, Zamba, and IBM Granite 4 follow the same hybrid pattern. The SSM layers keep a constant-size state so a long input does not blow up the KV-cache, giving large memory reductions and high long-context throughput, while the sparse attention layers handle exact retrieval — for example pulling a specific fact from far back in the context — that pure SSMs handle poorly. Quality stays near a comparable pure-attention model.
tldr: Hybrid SSM-Transformers interleave many constant-state SSM layers with a few attention layers. The SSM layers give cheap long-context throughput; the attention layers restore retrieval.

title: Latent Reasoning
short_definition: Reasoning carried in a model's continuous hidden states rather than emitted as text tokens; the canonical method feeds the last hidden state back as the next input embedding as a continuous thought.
full_explanation: Chain-of-thought reasoning forces every intermediate step through the discrete bottleneck of the vocabulary: the model must decode a token, then re-embed it, to continue thinking. Latent reasoning asks whether that detour is necessary, and proposes keeping the reasoning in the model's continuous hidden states instead of round-tripping through text. Meta's COCONUT is the canonical method: rather than decoding the next token, it feeds the model's last hidden state straight back in as the next input embedding — a continuous thought — and only emits text when the reasoning is done. It is trained with a curriculum that gradually replaces written chain-of-thought steps with these continuous thoughts, so the model learns to reason in latent space. Because a continuous thought is a vector rather than a single chosen token, it can hold several candidate reasoning paths in superposition at once, enabling a breadth-first-search-like exploration, and it can reach an answer in far fewer steps than token-level chain-of-thought. The costs are concrete: it needs special training, it does not run on stock serving stacks that assume token-by-token decoding, and there is no human-readable trace — which is in direct tension with chain-of-thought monitoring as a safety tool.
why_it_matters: If reasoning can live in continuous states, models could think more efficiently and explore multiple paths at once instead of committing to one token per step, which matters for hard search-like problems. But the same property removes the human-readable trace that chain-of-thought provides, and that trace is increasingly relied on for monitoring model reasoning, so latent reasoning sits at a genuine tension between capability and oversight. Knowing the tradeoff is essential before treating it as a free efficiency win.
example: COCONUT replaces decoded reasoning tokens with continuous thoughts — feeding the last hidden state back as the next input embedding — and trains this with a curriculum that swaps written chain-of-thought steps for latent ones over time. Because each continuous thought is a vector, it can represent multiple candidate paths simultaneously, giving a breadth-first-search-like behavior and reaching answers in fewer steps than token chain-of-thought. The price is no readable trace: an observer cannot inspect the latent steps the way they could read a written reasoning chain.
tldr: Latent reasoning keeps reasoning in continuous hidden states, not text; COCONUT feeds the last hidden state back as the next embedding. It explores many paths but leaves no readable trace.

title: Overthinking
short_definition: A failure mode where reasoning models spend large thinking budgets on problems that do not need them, lowering accuracy by second-guessing correct answers, with no benefit on easy ones.
full_explanation: Reasoning models can spend a long thinking budget before answering, which helps on hard problems but becomes a liability on easy ones. Overthinking is the failure mode where the model burns far more tokens than a question warrants — efficient-reasoning research through 2025 repeatedly found order-of-magnitude more tokens spent on trivial arithmetic with no accuracy gain, and worse, accuracy sometimes drops because the model talks itself out of a correct first answer. The mirror failure is underthinking: bailing out too early on genuinely hard problems. Both are about matching effort to difficulty, and getting it wrong costs latency and money on one side or correctness on the other. Mitigations work by capping or steering the thinking budget: explicit budgets such as Qwen3's thinking modes and Claude's extended-thinking budgets, budget forcing that cuts off or extends reasoning, length-penalized reinforcement learning that trains the model to be concise, and difficulty-aware routing that sends easy questions down a no-think path and hard ones down a thinking path. The key reframing is operational — overthinking is a latency and cost bug in production, not merely a quirk that shows up in benchmark token counts.

title: AIME (as an LLM Benchmark)
short_definition: The American Invitational Mathematics Examination — 15 questions per form, integer answers 0 to 999, two forms a year — repurposed as the standard competition-math benchmark for reasoning models.
full_explanation: AIME is a real high-school competition: each form has 15 questions, every answer is an integer from 0 to 999, and there are two forms per year. Those properties made it convenient to repurpose as an LLM benchmark for reasoning models. The integer-answer format means grading is a simple exact match — no judge model, no fuzzy comparison — which makes it ideal for verifiable-reward reinforcement learning, and that is partly why reasoning models saturated it so quickly. But the same small size that makes it clean also makes it statistically noisy: with only 15 problems per form and roughly 30 per year, a single lucky or unlucky question swings the score several points, so labs report averages over many samples (for example avg@64) rather than a single pass. There is also a contamination problem — older forms appear in pretraining data, so a model may have effectively memorized them — which is why you should always prefer the newest year's form. The trajectory is striking: DeepSeek-R1 reported 79.8% pass@1 on AIME-2024, and frontier 2025 reasoning models cleared 90%+ on AIME-2025.

The high variance from tiny problem counts means a single pass@1 number is unreliable, which is why credible reports average over many samples — and why comparing a model's avg@64 to another's single run is unfair. Contamination of older forms means a headline AIME score on a stale year can be inflated by memorization rather than reasoning, so the year matters as much as the number.

title: Logit Lens
short_definition: An interpretability technique that reads what a model currently predicts at an intermediate layer by pushing that layer's residual stream through the final LayerNorm and unembedding matrix.
full_explanation: A transformer builds its next-token prediction gradually across layers, but the prediction only becomes a distribution at the very end, after the final normalization and unembedding. The logit lens, introduced by nostalgebraist, asks what the model would predict if you stopped early: take the residual stream at any intermediate layer, push it through the same final LayerNorm and unembedding matrix the model uses at the output, and read off a token distribution. Doing this layer by layer reveals predictions sharpening as depth increases — an early guess that gets refined into the final answer — which is a concrete window into iterative refinement inside the network. It is the first tool to reach for before heavier interpretability methods like activation patching or sparse autoencoders, because it is cheap and needs no training. Its main weakness is conceptual: intermediate states are not actually trying to be final predictions, so reading them through the output head can produce garbage, especially in early layers of some models. The tuned lens, from Belrose and colleagues, fixes much of this by adding a small learned affine probe per layer, which corrects the early-layer distortions plain logit lens suffers.
why_it_matters: Logit lens turns the opaque stack of residual activations into something legible — you can watch a prediction form across depth, which is a fast way to build intuition about where in the network a behavior arises. As the cheapest interpretability probe, it is the natural first step before committing to expensive methods like patching or SAEs. Knowing its failure mode — and that the tuned lens repairs it — keeps you from over-trusting early-layer readouts.
example: Applying the logit lens across layers on a factual completion shows the correct token's probability rising layer by layer as the model refines its guess, illustrating iterative refinement directly. On some models the plain logit lens produces garbage in early layers because those residual states are not meant to be decoded by the output head; the tuned lens from Belrose and colleagues adds a small learned affine probe per layer that corrects this, giving cleaner early-layer readouts.
tldr: The logit lens reads an intermediate layer's prediction via the final LayerNorm and unembedding. It shows predictions sharpening with depth; the tuned lens adds probes to fix early-layer noise.

title: Induction Heads
short_definition: An attention-head circuit implementing copy-by-pattern: having seen a pair earlier, on encountering the first element again predict the second, built from a previous-token head and K-composition.
full_explanation: Induction heads are one of the clearest cases where mechanistic interpretability actually explains a model's behavior. The circuit implements a simple but general rule: if the sequence [A][B] appeared earlier, then when [A] shows up again, predict [B]. Named and characterized by Anthropic in work led by Olsson and colleagues, the circuit is built from two cooperating attention heads. A previous-token head writes, into each position, information about what came immediately before it; then the induction head reads that information through K-composition to attend from the second occurrence of [A] back to the [B] that followed the first [A], and copies it forward as the prediction. What makes them important is when they appear: they emerge in a sharp phase change early in training, and that phase change coincides with a jump in the model's in-context learning ability — strong evidence that much of in-context learning rides on induction-like circuits. They are found across model scales, which is why they became a staple demonstration that interpretability can pin a real, named mechanism to an observed capability rather than just describing it loosely.
why_it_matters: Induction heads are a rare existence proof that a specific, identifiable circuit underlies a high-level capability — in-context learning — which is central to how transformers learn from examples in the prompt. The fact that they emerge in a sharp training phase change tied to the in-context-learning jump links a mechanism to a behavior with unusual clarity. That makes them a foundational result for mechanistic interpretability and a common starting point for understanding what attention heads compute.

Mr D', an induction circuit attends from the second 'Mr D' back to where that pattern continued before and predicts the next token accordingly — copy-by-pattern in action. Mechanistically, a previous-token head tags each position with what preceded it, and the induction head uses K-composition to attend from the repeated token to the old continuation. Anthropic's analysis showed these heads emerge in a sharp phase change early in training that coincides with the model's jump in in-context learning ability.

title: Circuit Tracing (Attribution Graphs)
short_definition: Anthropic's 2025 method that replaces MLP computations with cross-layer transcoder features, then builds an attribution graph for one prompt showing which features causally feed which.
full_explanation: Sparse autoencoders give you a dictionary of interpretable features, but a dictionary does not tell you how features interact to produce a specific behavior. Circuit tracing, from Anthropic's 2025 work 'Circuit Tracing' and the companion 'On the Biology of a Large Language Model', closes that gap. The method swaps the model's MLP computations for cross-layer transcoder features — interpretable units that approximate what the MLPs do — and then, for one specific prompt, constructs an attribution graph: a directed graph showing which features causally feed which, traced all the way from input to output. The result is a mechanistic story for that single input rather than a static catalog. Run on Claude 3.5 Haiku, it surfaced concrete and sometimes surprising findings: genuine multi-step internal reasoning (for example computing Dallas to Texas to Austin rather than a direct lookup), forward planning in poetry where the model chooses the rhyme word before writing the line toward it, and circuits shared across languages. Anthropic open-sourced the approach as the circuit-tracer library. It is distinct from SAE work: SAEs find the dictionary of features, while attribution graphs trace how those features interact on a given input — and validation of the traced circuit still requires patching experiments to confirm the causal claims.
why_it_matters: Knowing a model's features is not the same as knowing how it thinks on a particular input, and circuit tracing supplies the missing interaction story. Its findings on Claude 3.5 Haiku — multi-step reasoning, forward planning in poetry, shared cross-lingual circuits — show models doing more structured internal computation than a next-token view suggests, which matters for both capability understanding and safety. Open-sourcing it as circuit-tracer lets the wider community probe models this way rather than taking such claims on faith.

The method builds an attribution graph over cross-layer transcoder features for that one prompt; confirming the graph's causal claims still requires patching experiments. Anthropic released it as the circuit-tracer library.

title: Glitch Tokens
short_definition: Tokens that exist in the vocabulary but are nearly absent from training data, leaving undertrained embeddings that trigger bizarre behavior — models cannot repeat them or hallucinate their meaning.
full_explanation: A tokenizer's vocabulary is fixed before training, and it is usually built on a corpus that does not perfectly match the data the model is later trained on. When some tokens end up in the vocabulary but almost never appear in training, their embeddings stay essentially undertrained — random-ish vectors the model never learned to use. Feeding such a glitch token in produces strange behavior: the model cannot repeat it back, hallucinates a meaning for it, or veers off entirely. The famous case is ' SolidGoldMagikarp' and a cluster of other Reddit-counting usernames that landed in the GPT-2/3 vocabulary, documented by Rumbelow and Watkins. The root cause is exactly that mismatch — the tokenizer was trained on a different corpus than the model, so certain merges never appeared during training. You detect them by looking for embedding-norm outliers and then confirming with verification prompts that ask the model to repeat or define the suspect token, a line of work nicknamed 'Fishing for Magikarp'. Mitigations are practical: audit the vocabulary before training to catch tokens with no training support, or filter the offending tokens at inference. There is a security angle too, since glitch tokens can be used to bypass filters or destabilize outputs.
why_it_matters: Glitch tokens are a concrete demonstration that the tokenizer is a real attack surface and failure source, not a neutral preprocessing step. A model that behaves bizarrely on certain inputs because their embeddings were never trained is a reliability problem, and the same tokens can be exploited to bypass content filters or destabilize generation, which is a security problem. Knowing to audit the vocabulary against the training corpus prevents shipping these latent landmines.

Rumbelow and Watkins documented this, and the detection recipe is to flag embedding-norm outliers, then confirm with verification prompts (the 'Fishing for Magikarp' line of work). The root cause was the tokenizer being trained on a different corpus than the model.

title: Model Checkpoint
short_definition: A saved snapshot of training state — the weights, and for resumable checkpoints also optimizer state, LR-schedule position, and data-loader state — used for crash recovery, branching, and release.
full_explanation: A long training run can take days or weeks across many GPUs, and anything can interrupt it, so you periodically save the state to disk. A model checkpoint is that snapshot. At minimum it holds the weights, but a resumable checkpoint also stores the optimizer state (for Adam, the running moment estimates), where you are in the learning-rate schedule, and the data-loader position, so a restarted run continues exactly where it left off rather than starting over. Checkpoints serve several purposes: crash recovery, branching experiments from a common point, evaluating how capability evolves over training time, rolling back after a loss spike, and ultimately the artifact you release. Confusingly, 'checkpoint' colloquially also means released weights — the safetensors files you download from a model hub — which are inference-only and much smaller. The size gap is worth understanding: a training checkpoint under mixed-precision training keeps fp32 master weights plus two Adam moment tensors, so it is roughly four times the size of the bf16 weights alone before any sharding. Related practices include checkpoint averaging or model soups, where multiple checkpoints are combined, and keeping EMA weights for release.
why_it_matters: Checkpoints are the safety net and the version-control system of training — without them a single crash wastes days of compute, and branching, ablations, and rollbacks all depend on having clean snapshots. The distinction between a heavy resumable training checkpoint and a light inference-only release checkpoint affects storage planning and what you actually ship. The roughly 4x size factor from optimizer state explains why training storage budgets dwarf the size of the final released model.
example: Under mixed-precision training with Adam, a checkpoint that must resume training keeps fp32 master weights plus two moment tensors — roughly four times the size of the bf16 weights — whereas the released safetensors file holds only the inference weights and is far smaller. A team might checkpoint every few thousand steps so that after a loss spike they can roll back to the last good snapshot, branch a data-mixture ablation from a shared checkpoint, and later release an EMA-averaged or souped version of several late checkpoints.
tldr: A model checkpoint is a saved snapshot of training state: weights, and for resuming also optimizer and schedule state. Training checkpoints are roughly 4x the weight size; released ones smaller.

Confusingly, 'checkpoint' colloquially also means released weights — the safetensors files you download from a model hub — which are inference-only and much smaller.

Related practices include checkpoint averaging or model soups, where multiple checkpoints are combined, and keeping EMA weights for release.
pitfalls: A weights-only checkpoint cannot resume training faithfully — without optimizer state, LR-schedule position, and data-loader state, the restart diverges from the original trajectory. People underestimate storage because training checkpoints are roughly 4x the released model size thanks to fp32 master weights and Adam moments. And the word 'checkpoint' is overloaded: a released inference checkpoint and a resumable training checkpoint are very different artifacts, so conflating them leads to wrong size and capability assumptions.
when: Save checkpoints throughout any non-trivial training run for crash recovery, rollback, branching, and to evaluate capability over time, keeping resumable state if you may need to continue. For pure inference and distribution you only need the lighter weights-only release checkpoint, not the full optimizer-bearing snapshot.

faq.a: Optimizer state (for Adam, the moment estimates), the learning-rate-schedule position, and the data-loader state. Those let a restarted run continue on the same trajectory instead of effectively starting a new one.

title: Context Compaction
short_definition: Replacing older conversation and tool history in a long agent session with a structured summary of task-critical state, then continuing in the freed-up context window.
full_explanation: A long-running agent eventually fills its context window with transcript: every tool call, every file dump, every dead end. Truncation drops the oldest tokens blindly and can throw away a constraint you still need. Compaction instead reads the history and rewrites it into a compact summary that pins down what the session is actually carrying — the goal, decisions already made, file paths, constraints, and open TODOs — and the agent continues from that summary with most of the window back. Claude Code popularized the pattern with its /compact command and automatic compaction near the limit. It differs from external memory, which stores facts and recalls them on demand rather than rewriting the live transcript. The trigger is usually a context-budget threshold: when used tokens cross a watermark, the agent (or the harness) pauses normal work. A compaction prompt asks the model to produce a structured summary keyed to the task — typically 'what we are doing, why, what is done, what is next, and the key artifacts and their paths.' The old turns are dropped from the active window and replaced by that summary. Work resumes against the summary plus whatever recent turns were kept verbatim. Good compaction prompts force the model to name concrete state; weak ones produce vague prose that loses the constraints the agent needed.
why_it_matters: Without compaction a long agent run either dies at the context limit or silently forgets why it started. Compaction is what lets a coding agent work for an extended session across many files without losing the plot. But it is lossy: a single bad compaction can drop a hard requirement, and repeated compaction compounds summary drift, so the prompt that writes the summary is load-bearing.
example: Claude Code hits roughly 95% of its context window during a multi-file refactor. Auto-compaction fires: the prior 60+ turns of tool output get replaced by a structured summary listing the goal (migrate auth to the new SDK), files already changed, the test command, and the remaining TODO list. The agent continues with most of the window freed, still aware of the constraint that the public API must not change — because the compaction prompt explicitly pinned constraints.
tldr: When a long agent session nears its context limit, compaction rewrites old history into a structured summary of goals, decisions, paths, and TODOs, then continues with the window freed.
